intro: Documents the Ben Born Again channel (youtube.com/@1BENBORNAGAIN) and its website, benbornagain.faith, talk about. Each has a short description; where the channel says something about a document, that is given separately under “What the channel says”, in summary and as the channel’s own view.

groups.title: The Old Testament: Septuagint and Masoretic text
groups.about: The channel’s main subject: which Old Testament text to trust, the Greek Septuagint (LXX) or the Hebrew Masoretic text (MT).

groups.title: Early Bibles
groups.about: The Bibles the channel holds up as coming from reliable manuscripts, and the earliest English Bible it mentions.

groups.title: Early church writings
groups.about: Christian writings from about AD 96–160. The channel quotes 1 Clement; the others are the rest of the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament, included for comparison.

groups.title: Historians
groups.about: Writers outside the Bible the channel cites as evidence for Jesus.

groups.title: Texts the channel warns about
groups.about: Books the channel criticizes and warns Christians against. They are included as historical documents, so you can read what is being discussed, not as recommendations.

missing: Some documents the channel cites can’t be included, because the translations it uses are still under copyright or no free copy could be found: the Dead Sea Scrolls, Aryeh Kaplan’s edition of the Sefer Yetzirah, the Soncino Zohar and Talmud, Shem Tov’s Hebrew Matthew, Tyndale’s 1525 New Testament, Pliny’s letter about the Christians (Betty Radice’s translation), and the modern books and articles it quotes.

documents.title: The Septuagint in English (Brenton)
documents.by: Translated by Sir Lancelot C. L. Brenton
documents.about: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made by Jewish scholars in Alexandria, beginning with the Law in the 3rd century BC and finished over the next two centuries. The New Testament often quotes it. This is Brenton’s English translation with the books the Septuagint has beyond the Hebrew Bible, in the LXX2012 edition, which modernizes some spelling and words. Chapters and verses follow the Septuagint, so most Psalms are numbered one lower than in the King James Version (its Psalm 22 is the KJV’s Psalm 23), and Jeremiah is arranged differently.
documents.channel: The channel’s main source; it uses Brenton’s translation. It holds that the Septuagint, which it dates to about 285 BC at the request of King Ptolemy II, is the Old Testament Jesus and the apostles quoted, about 90% of the time by its count. It says the Masoretic Hebrew text behind most modern Old Testaments, including the KJV’s, was finalized around AD 1000 and changed passages that point to Christ. Its examples: Psalm 40:6 (quoted in Hebrews 10:5), Deuteronomy 32:43 (Hebrews 1:6), Isaiah 61:1 (Luke 4:18), Job 2:9, Proverbs 24:21–22 and the ages in Genesis 5 and 11.
documents.credit: Brenton’s translation (1844, public domain), LXX2012 edition by Michael Paul Johnson, eBible.org (public domain).

documents.title: The Masoretic text (Hebrew)
documents.about: The Hebrew Old Testament as standardized by the Masoretes, Jewish scribes who added vowels and accents between about AD 600 and 1000. The Leningrad Codex is the oldest complete manuscript of it; nearly all Hebrew Bibles and most English Old Testaments, including the KJV, are based on this text. Where it differs from the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls (copied between about 250 BC and AD 70) sometimes agree with the Septuagint and more often with the Masoretic text. In Hebrew, read right to left.
documents.channel: The channel calls the Masoretic text “Hebrew 2.0” and says it was finalized around AD 1000 and altered verses about Jesus, which is why it prefers the Septuagint. It shows the Leningrad Codex as its example of the Masoretic text.
documents.credit: Westminster Leningrad Codex (public domain), text as published by the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible project, github.com/openscriptures/morphhb.

documents.title: The Geneva Bible
documents.about: The English Bible of the Reformation, translated by Protestants in exile in Geneva and first published in 1560. It was the Bible of Shakespeare, John Bunyan and the Pilgrims. This is the 1599 printing in its original spelling (heauen for heaven, vpon for upon), without its notes and Apocrypha.
documents.channel: The channel names the 1560 Geneva Bible, with the original 1611 King James Bible, as English Bibles from the “Antioch” line of New Testament manuscripts that it trusts, and points out that both included the Apocrypha.
documents.credit: Geneva Bible 1599 (public domain), from CrossWire’s SWORD module as converted by scrollmapper bible_databases (github.com/scrollmapper/bible_databases).

documents.title: The Apocrypha of the 1611 King James Bible
documents.about: The 14 books printed between the Old and New Testaments in the original 1611 King James Bible, in the 1769 text used by Quiet Bible’s KJV. Most of them are in the Septuagint. Most English Protestant Bibles left them out from the 1800s on.
documents.channel: The channel points out that the original 1611 King James Bible and the Geneva Bible included these books, and that Brenton’s Septuagint has them too. It distinguishes them from the “Gnostic” apocryphal books, which it rejects.
documents.credit: King James Version with Apocrypha (1769 text, public domain), from the scrollmapper bible_databases KJVA text as collected by Open Christian Data.

documents.title: The Textus Receptus (Greek New Testament)
documents.about: The printed Greek New Testament of the Reformation, first edited by Erasmus in 1516, behind the Geneva Bible and the King James Version. This is the Textus Receptus as printed by Stephanus in 1550 and by Scrivener in 1894. In Greek.
documents.channel: The channel holds the Textus Receptus to be the reliable Greek New Testament. It says modern Bibles such as the NASB and ESV follow “Alexandrian” manuscripts instead, which it regards as corrupted and blames on Origen of Alexandria.
documents.credit: Textus Receptus (1550/1894, public domain), from CrossWire’s SWORD module as converted by scrollmapper bible_databases.

documents.title: The Wycliffe Bible
documents.about: The first complete Bible in English, translated from the Latin Vulgate in the Middle English of the 1380s and 1390s, with the books the Vulgate has beyond the Hebrew Bible and the Epistle to the Laodiceans.
documents.channel: Mentioned on the channel’s site as an English Bible from before the King James, in its discussion of the names Jesus and Yeshua.
documents.credit: Wycliffe Bible (about 1395, public domain), from CrossWire’s SWORD module as converted by scrollmapper bible_databases.

documents.title: 1 Clement
documents.about: A letter from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth, traditionally by Clement, bishop of Rome, written about AD 96. It is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament.
documents.channel: The channel quotes chapter 12, where Clement retells Rahab’s words, “the Lord your God hath given you this city”, using the Greek word kyrios, Lord. It takes this as evidence that the first Christians said “Lord”, not a Hebrew name such as YHWH.
documents.credit: Translation by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: 2 Clement
documents.about: A sermon long attributed to Clement of Rome but by an unknown author; the oldest Christian sermon outside the New Testament.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: The Didache
documents.about: “The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles”, a short early church manual: the way of life and the way of death, baptism, fasting, prayer and the Lord’s Supper. It was rediscovered in 1873.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1886, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: The Epistle of Barnabas
documents.about: A letter under the name of Paul’s companion Barnabas that reads the Old Testament, its sacrifices, Sabbath and food laws, as pointing to Christ. It is included in Codex Sinaiticus.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: The Letters of Ignatius
documents.about: Seven letters written by Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom in Rome. The Ante-Nicene Fathers gives two versions of each, a shorter one generally held to be original and a longer one expanded in the 4th century; here each passage of the shorter version comes first, followed by the longer one.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: Polycarp
documents.by: Polycarp of Smyrna; the church of Smyrna
documents.about: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the apostle John, wrote his letter to the Philippians in the early 2nd century. The Martyrdom of Polycarp tells of his death in about AD 155 and is the oldest Christian account of a martyrdom outside the New Testament.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: The Epistle to Diognetus
documents.about: An anonymous defence of the Christian faith, addressed to an inquirer named Diognetus, describing Christians as “the soul of the world”.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: The Shepherd of Hermas
documents.about: A book of visions, commandments and parables written in Rome and widely read in the early church; it is included in Codex Sinaiticus.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: Justin Martyr
documents.about: Justin, a philosopher who became a Christian and was martyred in Rome around AD 165. In the First Apology he defends Christians to the emperor. In the Dialogue with Trypho he debates a Jewish teacher; in chapters 71–73 he defends the Septuagint and accuses Jewish teachers of his day of rejecting or removing some of its readings about Christ, the same question the channel raises.
documents.credit: Ante-Nicene Fathers (1885, public domain), from the Historical Christian Faith Writings Database.

documents.title: The Works of Josephus
documents.by: Flavius Josephus; translated by William Whiston
documents.about: Josephus (AD 37–about 100) was a Jewish priest and commander in the war against Rome who then wrote its history under Roman patronage: The Wars of the Jews, the Antiquities of the Jews (a history from Creation to his own day), his Life, and Against Apion. The passage about Jesus, the “Testimonium Flavianum”, is in Antiquities, Book 18, chapter 3. Most scholars think it is genuine at its core but was added to by later Christian copyists.
documents.channel: The channel quotes Antiquities 18.3.3, the Testimonium Flavianum, as evidence for Jesus, and cites Josephus for Herod, Philip, Annas and Caiaphas.
documents.credit: William Whiston’s translation (1737, public domain), as transcribed by sacred-texts.com.

documents.title: Tacitus on Christ (Annals 15.44)
documents.by: Tacitus; translated by A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb
documents.about: The Roman historian Tacitus on how Nero blamed the Christians for the great fire of Rome in AD 64, with his note that “Christus” was executed under Tiberius by Pontius Pilate.
documents.channel: The channel quotes this passage, in this translation, as Roman evidence that Jesus was a real person executed under Pilate.
documents.credit: Church and Brodribb’s translation (1876, public domain), as transcribed by sacred-texts.com.

documents.title: The Babylonian Talmud (Rodkinson)
documents.by: Translated and edited by Michael L. Rodkinson
documents.about: The central text of rabbinic Judaism: the Mishnah, a written collection of the oral law from about AD 200, and the Gemara, later rabbis’ discussion of it, completed in Babylonia around AD 500. Rodkinson’s edition covers only some tractates and shortens and rearranges them, so it is not a complete or exact translation.
documents.channel: The channel warns against the Talmud. It says the Talmud codifies the “oral law”, which it identifies with the “tradition of the elders” that Jesus condemned in Mark 7:5–13, and it warns Christians against the Hebrew Roots movement’s turn to rabbinic tradition and Torah observance.
documents.warning: Included as a historical document, not as Scripture.
documents.credit: Rodkinson’s translation (1896–1903, public domain in the United States), as scanned and proofed by sacred-texts.com (J. B. Hare). The archive’s notice on Books 1 and 4 asks that the attribution be kept and those two books used only for non-commercial purposes.
documents.license: Public domain in the United States; Books 1 and 4 are for non-commercial use only and are not covered by Quiet Bible’s GPL licence

documents.title: The Zohar (partial)
documents.about: The foundational book of Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism: a mystical commentary on the Torah written in Aramaic. It appeared in Spain in the 1280s through Moses de León, who attributed it to the 2nd-century rabbi Simeon bar Yochai. This is the only English translation old enough to be free, and it covers only the opening portion, on Genesis 1–12. The translator wrote for a Theosophist magazine.
documents.channel: The channel warns against Kabbalah, which it calls “the religion of the serpent”, as occult and opposed to the gospel. It describes the Zohar as Kabbalah’s main book, in 23 books, attributed to Moses de León (1240–1305).
documents.warning: Occult and mystical material. Included as a historical document, not as Scripture or for practice.
documents.credit: Nurho de Manhar’s translation (1900–1914, public domain in the United States), as scanned and proofed by sacred-texts.com (J. B. Hare), whose notice asks that the attribution be kept and the text used only for non-commercial purposes.
documents.license: Public domain in the United States; for non-commercial use only, and not covered by Quiet Bible’s GPL licence

documents.title: The Sefer Yetzirah
documents.date: between the 2nd and 6th centuries AD; translation 1887
documents.about: “The Book of Formation”, a short early Jewish text on how God made the world through ten numbers (the sefirot) and the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet; it became a foundation of Kabbalah. The translator, Westcott, was a founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, an occult society.
documents.channel: The channel lists the Sefer Yetzirah among the Kabbalistic books it warns about, citing Aryeh Kaplan’s modern edition, and connects Kabbalah with occult practices such as the legend of making a golem.
documents.warning: Occult and mystical material. Included as a historical document, not as Scripture or for practice.
documents.credit: Westcott’s translation (1887, public domain), as transcribed by sacred-texts.com.

documents.title: The Lesser Key of Solomon (Goetia)
documents.by: Edited by S. L. MacGregor Mathers and Aleister Crowley
documents.about: A 17th-century book of ritual magic, falsely attributed to King Solomon. Its first part, the Goetia, lists 72 spirits it calls demons and gives rituals for summoning them. This edition was prepared by two of the best-known occultists of their day. Its seals and diagrams are not included.
documents.channel: The channel names this as the book that summons demons by 72 names, and links it to the Kabbalistic “72 names of God” (Shem HaMephorash) and to occult use of the Tetragrammaton, which it says is one reason it does not use the name YHWH.
documents.warning: A manual of ritual magic and summoning, which the Bible forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Included only as a historical document, so you can see what the channel is warning about.
documents.credit: Mathers and Crowley’s edition (1904, public domain), as scanned and proofed by sacred-texts.com (J. B. Hare).
